questions.prompt: f(θ)=½λθ² with λ=2, η=0.75, θ₀=1. What is θ₃? (decimal, tolerance 0.0005)
A loss has largest curvature λ_max=8 in the relevant region. What is the largest stable learning rate (the boundary, as a decimal, tolerance 0.001)?
A run's loss goes 0.8, 3.1, 12.9, 51, 204 with weights flipping sign each step. What is the most likely cause?
options: The model is underfitting; increase the batch size.
The weights were initialized too large; the loss will recover by itself.
The data split is too small to train on.
The learning rate exceeds 2/λ_max in the sign-flipping direction.
questions.explanation: Geometric growth with alternating sign is the signature (1−ηλ)^t with 1−ηλ<−1.

questions.prompt: 60000 training images, batch size 256, last short batch kept. How many iterations per epoch? (integer, tolerance 0.01)
questions.explanation: 60000/256=234.4, rounded up to 235 (the last batch holds 96 images).

questions.prompt: N=1050, B=100, 12 epochs, last short batch kept. How many parameter updates in total? (integer, tolerance 0.01)
A tanh layer has 300 inputs and 100 outputs. Xavier/Glorot weight std = sqrt(2/(n_in+n_out)). Give it as a decimal (tolerance 0.001).
A 30-layer ReLU network is initialized with weight std 0.01 in every layer (n_in=256). What do you expect at the output at step 0?
options: Activations explode to huge values, since small weights get amplified layer by layer.
Activations shrink layer by layer to almost zero, so the loss starts flat and gradients vanish.
Nothing unusual: small weights are always safe and give stable, well-scaled activations.
All units become identical, because the small weights make every neuron compute the same value.
questions.explanation: Each layer multiplies the std by about 0.01·sqrt(256/2)=0.11, so after 30 layers the signal is ~10^-29. He std here is 0.088.

questions.prompt: Single-sample gradient std σ=6. What is the standard deviation of a minibatch gradient with B=144? (decimal, tolerance 0.001)
Which statement about minibatch gradients is a misconception?
options: Noise can help escape sharp regions, which is one reason small batches are used.
With uniform sampling the minibatch gradient is an unbiased estimate of the full gradient.
Doubling B reduces noise std by a factor of √2.
A larger batch makes the gradient estimate biased toward large-loss samples.
questions.explanation: Batch size changes variance, not bias; uniform sampling keeps the expectation equal to the full gradient.

questions.prompt: Two learning rates are compared; run A uses split 1 and seed 0, run B uses split 2 and seed 7. A wins by 1.5 points. What is the best description?
options: The comparison is valid because both runs trained for the same number of epochs, so the budget was equal.
The comparison is only invalid if the test set was also used to tune the learning rate.
The comparison is confounded: split and seed differ, so the gap cannot be attributed to the learning rate.
The comparison is valid because a 1.5 point gap is large enough to ignore the split and seed.
questions.explanation: A controlled comparison changes one factor. Different splits and seeds add variance of unknown size.

questions.prompt: Your loss becomes nan at step 40 with learning rate 0.5. List, in order, three checks you would run before changing the architecture, and what each would tell you.
rubric: Reruns with a much smaller learning rate (e.g. 10x lower) to test whether it is a stability issue.
Checks the loss/gradient scale: mean vs sum over the batch, unnormalised inputs, bad labels or inf in data.
Runs a tiny overfit test or gradient check on one batch with a fixed seed to separate a bug from a hyperparameter problem.
questions.explanation: Rubric-guided: compare your answer with each rubric point; this question is not automatically graded.

questions.prompt: Write (in words or pseudocode) how you make a training loop reproducible: where each seed is set, what is shuffled and when, and what you save with the result.
rubric: Creates one seeded random generator for init and one for shuffling, set before training, never reseeded inside the epoch loop.
Fixes the train/validation/test split once (saved indices or a seed) and reshuffles training indices every epoch.
Saves seed, learning rate, batch size, epochs, split, code version and final metrics with the result.
questions.explanation: Rubric-guided: compare your answer with each rubric point; this question is not automatically graded.

questions.prompt: A quadratic has curvatures 2 and 14. With the best constant learning rate 2/(λ_min+λ_max), what is the per-step contraction factor of the error (decimal, tolerance 0.001)?

A quadratic has curvatures between μ and L with condition number κ=L/μ=64. With the optimal heavy-ball (momentum) parameters, what is the asymptotic per-step contraction factor (decimal, tolerance 0.001)?
questions.explanation: The optimal heavy-ball rate is √β*=(√κ−1)/(√κ+1)=(8−1)/(8+1)=7/9≈0.7778. Plain gradient descent would give (κ−1)/(κ+1)=63/65≈0.969, i.e. roughly κ instead of √κ steps for a fixed accuracy.

questions.prompt: On f(θ)=½λθ² with λ=1.5, SGD uses η=0.4 and a minibatch gradient with noise variance σ²/B=36/9=4 (σ=6, B=9), independent across steps. What is the stationary expected loss E[f(θ)] (decimal, tolerance 0.001)?
questions.explanation: With a=1−ηλ=0.4, V=a²V+η²·4 gives V=0.64/0.84=0.7619. The expected loss is ½λV=0.5714, which equals ησ²/(2B(2−ηλ))=0.4·36/(2·9·1.4). The iteration is stable (|a|<1) but the loss stays at this noise floor.

questions.prompt: A team trains with plain minibatch SGD at a small learning rate (ηλ ≪ 1 along every direction) and raises the batch size from 32 to 128, keeping the learning rate and everything else. What do you expect from the stationary training loss (the noise floor)?
options: Roughly unchanged, because the expected gradient does not depend on B.
Roughly one quarter of its old value: the floor is proportional to η/B.
Roughly one half of its old value, because the noise std falls like 1/√B.
Higher, because fewer updates are made per epoch.
questions.explanation: The stationary loss is ησ²/(2B(2−ηλ)) ≈ ησ²/(4B) for small ηλ, so it is inversely proportional to B: quadrupling the batch divides the floor by about 4. The noise standard deviation does halve (1/√B), but the loss floor scales with the variance, which is why the "one half" option is wrong. The expected gradient is unchanged but that does not make the floor unchanged. Fewer updates per epoch changes the speed of reaching the floor, not its height.
questions.skillLabel: Batch size and the SGD noise floor
